messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Duc was fifty-one, a policy analyst for a state transportation agency, when the wildfire came through the canyon where he had lived for twenty years. He had been home alone on a Tuesday afternoon, reviewing a draft environmental impact report at his kitchen table, when the smoke alarm on the first floor began to chirp. He assumed it was a false signal—the battery had been dying for days—but the smell that followed was not electrical. It was thick and sweet, like a campfire someone had doused with gasoline. He walked to the window and saw the ridge behind his house glowing orange. The evacuation order came over his phone thirty seconds later, and in the chaos of grabbing his laptop and his go-bag, he lost his glasses, his car keys, and, for a long, terrifying moment, his sense of which way the driveway faced. The fire did not reach his home—firefighters stopped it a quarter-mile away—but the evacuation lasted three days, and when he returned, the air still tasted of ash.

In the weeks that followed, Duc found himself scanning the horizon whenever he drove home from work, checking for smoke that was not there. He began to avoid the canyon route entirely, taking a longer highway that added twenty minutes to his commute. At the office, he started to notice that his hands would tremble when a colleague walked into his cubicle without warning. Unpredictable situations—a sudden meeting room booking, a fire drill, a child’s birthday party with a piñata that produced a puff of confetti—made his chest tighten and his vision narrow. He had always been the reliable one in his team, the analyst who caught the errors in other people’s spreadsheets. Now he found himself double-checking his own work three or four times, certain he had missed something catastrophic. When his supervisor asked why he had not submitted a routine quarterly report on time, Duc heard the question as an accusation and spent the rest of the day convinced he was about to be fired. He told himself that his reactions since the fire meant he was going crazy, that his mind had broken in a way that could not be fixed. He had come to believe that he could not rely on himself anymore—that his own judgment, the very thing his job depended on, was no longer trustworthy. What frightened him most was the thought that if he let his guard down, even for a moment, he would miss the next sign of danger and something far worse would happen. He became certain that he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next.

The connection between these fears and his triggers tightened into a loop he could not escape. A minor headache—feeling physically unwell in any way—would send him into a spiral of checking his body for symptoms, certain that the dizziness meant carbon monoxide or a stroke. That spiral would confirm, in his mind, that he could not rely on himself to stay calm, which made him even more vigilant, scanning for the next unpredictable threat. The smell of smoke from a neighbor’s grill, or even the faint burnt-toast odor from the office toaster, would bring the canyon afternoon back so vividly that he would have to excuse himself to the restroom and stand with his hands on the sink until his breathing slowed. Each time he reacted that way, he felt more convinced that he was losing his grip, and that conviction made the next trigger hit even harder. He stopped going to the grocery store on weekends because the crowds felt unpredictable. He stopped driving his son to soccer practice because a sudden lane change by another driver made him pull over and shake. His wife noticed that he was quieter at dinner, that he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind.

What finally brought Duc to seek help was a Tuesday afternoon exactly one year after the fire. He was at his desk, and a maintenance worker began testing the fire alarms in the hallway. The sound was shrill and sudden, and Duc dropped his coffee, stood up, and walked out of the building without telling anyone. He stood in the parking lot for twenty minutes, unable to go back inside. He was afraid that if he returned to his desk, he would have to admit to himself that he was no longer the person he had been. He was more afraid, though, of staying the same.
